result: The study used a retrospective cohort design with 7,906,603 patients from a large US insurance claims database (Komodo Health) covering January 2019 to June 2020. Bisphosphonate users (n=450,366) were identified based on claims during a 14-month pre-observation period and 1:1 propensity score-matched to non-users by age, gender, insurance type, PCP visit, and comorbidity burden, with matching performed within geographic regions. Primary and secondary endpoints (COVID-19 hospitalization, diagnosis, and SARS-CoV-2 testing) were defined using specific ICD-10 and CPT codes.
evaluation: The study design, data source, cohort selection, matching methodology, and endpoint definitions are clearly described with appropriate operational definitions (C1-C5, C32-C47). The propensity score matching achieved excellent balance with >98% of matches having propensity score differences <0.000001 (C61), and the large sample size provides adequate statistical power. The methodology is transparent and reproducible.

result: Before propensity score matching, BP users differed significantly from non-users: they were older (82.7% vs 27.7% age >60), predominantly female (91.0% vs 57.2%), and had higher comorbidity burden (mean CCI 0.95 vs 0.60). After matching 450,366 BP users to 450,366 non-users, demographic characteristics were balanced, though BP non-users had higher rates of several comorbidities including COPD (10.2% vs 8.5%), cardiovascular disease (25.1% vs 18.7%), and type 2 diabetes (22.9% vs 18.2%).
evaluation: The pre-match differences (C51-C53) and post-match balance (C54, C61) are clearly documented with statistical tests. However, the residual imbalances in individual comorbidities after matching (C55-C60) represent a limitation that could confound results, though these were controlled for in regression analyses. The matching quality metrics (C61) demonstrate excellent technical execution of the propensity score matching.

result: In the primary matched cohort, BP users had dramatically reduced odds of all COVID-19-related outcomes compared to non-users: SARS-CoV-2 testing (adjusted OR=0.22, 95%CI:0.21-0.23), COVID-19 diagnosis (adjusted OR=0.23, 95%CI:0.22-0.24), and COVID-19-related hospitalization (adjusted OR=0.26, 95%CI:0.24-0.29), all p<0.001. These associations remained robust across geographic regions and in New York state alone, representing a three- to five-fold reduction in incidence.
evaluation: While the statistical associations are strong and consistent (C6-C8, C62-C68), the observational study design cannot establish causation. Critical confounders include: (1) potential differences in SARS-CoV-2 exposure between groups that cannot be measured from claims data; (2) racial/ethnic composition differences that may affect both BP prescription patterns and COVID-19 risk; (3) socioeconomic factors not fully captured by insurance type; (4) the 'healthy adherer effect' where BP users may have healthier behaviors overall; and (5) residual confounding from comorbidity imbalances after matching (C55-C60). The reduced testing rates (C62) may reflect milder symptoms rather than true protection, leading to detection bias for diagnosis and hospitalization outcomes.

result: Timing analyses revealed that BP users had decreased odds of COVID-19 outcomes regardless of when they last received BP therapy, including those whose alendronic acid prescription ended >8 months before the observation period and those who newly initiated therapy immediately before the observation period. The only exceptions were zoledronic acid users last dosed in January/February 2019 (hospitalization OR=0.52, p=0.20) or newly initiated in February 2020 (hospitalization OR=0.49, p=0.30), which were not statistically significant.
evaluation: The timing analysis (C69-C70, C145-C146) suggests long-lasting effects consistent with BP bone retention (C147-C148), but the lack of dose-response relationship and protection even with distant or very recent exposure raises questions about the biological plausibility of a direct drug effect. The non-significant findings for certain zoledronic acid subgroups may reflect small sample sizes rather than true lack of effect. Alternative explanations such as unmeasured confounding related to patient characteristics that determine BP prescription timing cannot be excluded.

result: Two sensitivity analyses comparing BP users to users of other anti-resorptive medications showed consistent results. In the 'Bone-Rx' cohort (BP users vs non-BP anti-resorptive medication users), BP users had decreased odds of testing (OR=0.31), diagnosis (OR=0.35), and hospitalization (OR=0.45), all p<0.001. In the more restrictive 'Osteo-Dx-Rx' cohort (female patients >50 with osteoporosis diagnosis from high-incidence states), BP users maintained decreased odds of testing (OR=0.28), diagnosis (OR=0.40), and hospitalization (OR=0.45, p=0.003).
evaluation: These sensitivity analyses (C71-C76) strengthen the findings by comparing to more similar control groups, partially addressing confounding by indication. However, the 'Bone-Rx' cohort still showed residual confounding with different comorbidity profiles between BP and non-BP anti-resorptive users. The 'Osteo-Dx-Rx' cohort is more restrictive but has much smaller sample size (n=15,898 total), limiting power and generalizability. The consistent direction of effects across analyses is notable, but cannot definitively rule out unmeasured confounding related to why clinicians chose BPs over other anti-resorptive medications.

result: BP use was associated with decreased odds of other respiratory infections in 2019 (pre-COVID): acute bronchitis (OR range 0.23-0.28) and pneumonia (OR range 0.32-0.36) across all cohort variations. This suggests BPs may protect against respiratory infections from multiple pathogens, not just SARS-CoV-2.
evaluation: The associations with pre-COVID respiratory infections (C9-C10, C77-C78, C86) provide important context suggesting a broader protective effect rather than COVID-19-specific mechanisms. This is consistent with prior literature (C85) and strengthens biological plausibility. However, the same confounding issues apply: BP users may have different healthcare-seeking behavior, exposure patterns, or unmeasured characteristics that reduce respiratory infection risk independent of drug effects. The consistency across multiple respiratory pathogens (C87) is intriguing but does not establish causation.

result: Comparisons with other preventive medication classes (statins, antihypertensives, antidiabetics, antidepressants) showed that these drugs had much weaker associations with COVID-19 outcomes than BPs. When BP use was assessed within matched cohorts of other preventive medication users/non-users, BP use remained consistently associated with lower odds of testing (OR 0.21-0.27), diagnosis (OR 0.22-0.30), and hospitalization (OR 0.25-0.33). Notably, statin users had similar odds of COVID-19 hospitalization as non-users despite racial/ethnic minorities being under-represented in both statin and BP user populations.
evaluation: This sensitivity analysis (C79-C82) attempts to address the 'healthy adherer effect' by showing that other preventive medications don't show similar associations, and that BP effects persist within other medication user groups. However, the analysis assumes that unmeasured confounders affect all preventive medications similarly, which may not be true. Different medications are prescribed for different indications and patient populations. The statin comparison (C100-C101) is particularly relevant since statins and BPs share some mechanistic pathways, yet show different COVID-19 associations, but this could reflect differences in patient populations or prescribing patterns rather than true drug effects.

result: The authors address potential confounding by race/ethnicity by noting that Black/African-American and Hispanic patients have higher COVID-19 rates and that BP users may be disproportionately non-Hispanic White. Using California data, they estimate race-adjusted COVID-19 incidence would be 1.7% for BP users vs 2.1% for non-users, compared to actual observed rates of 0.46% vs 2.5% in the Western US. They argue that racial composition differences cannot fully explain the observed associations, and that testing rates show similar racial proportions to the general population.
evaluation: The race/ethnicity analysis (C91-C99, C105-C106) attempts to address an important confounder but has significant limitations. The race-adjustment calculation (C97) relies on external California data and makes strong assumptions about the racial composition of the study cohorts, which is not directly measured in the claims data. The comparison of estimated (1.7% vs 2.1%) to observed (0.46% vs 2.5%) rates (C98-C99) shows a large unexplained difference that could reflect unmeasured confounding. The argument about testing rates (C105-C106) doesn't address whether BP users and non-users had similar exposure risk to SARS-CoV-2, which is the critical unmeasured confounder. Without direct measurement of race/ethnicity and SARS-CoV-2 exposure in the study population, this remains a major limitation.

result: The authors propose that reduced testing rates among BP users may reflect milder or absent symptoms due to enhanced antiviral immune responses, leading to 'silent' infections that were not captured. They argue that potential misclassification biases (false COVID-19 diagnoses without testing, BP non-users receiving BPs during observation, censoring due to death) would bias results toward the null and do not explain the observed associations.
evaluation: The proposed mechanism (C107-C109) is speculative and represents an alternative interpretation of the reduced testing rates rather than evidence for BP efficacy. The 'silent infection' hypothesis cannot be tested with the available data and could alternatively reflect differential healthcare-seeking behavior or exposure risk. The bias analyses (C110-C113) are appropriate and show that identified biases would attenuate rather than create the observed associations, which is reassuring. However, these analyses don't address the fundamental limitation that unmeasured confounding could create spurious associations in the same direction as a true drug effect.

result: The authors conclude that the consistency and strength of associations across multiple analytical approaches support that BPs should be considered for prophylactic use in individuals at risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection, but acknowledge that prospective clinical trials are required to establish causation and determine the true magnitude of effects.
evaluation: The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitations of observational data (C12, C84, C142) and correctly state that causation cannot be established without prospective trials. The recommendation to 'consider' BPs for prophylactic use (C141) is appropriately cautious given the strength of associations and consistency across analyses (C140), but the evidence remains insufficient to support actual clinical implementation without randomized trials. The conclusion appropriately balances the intriguing observational findings with the need for definitive evidence.

result: The introduction establishes that bisphosphonates are small-molecule drugs that inhibit bone resorption, are widely prescribed for osteoporosis and other bone conditions, and are subdivided into amino-BPs and non-amino-BPs with distinct mechanisms. BPs exert immunomodulatory effects including regulation of γδT cells, neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, with prior observational studies showing reduced pneumonia incidence and mortality. BPs are globally accessible as affordable generics with known safety profiles.
evaluation: The background information on BP pharmacology, clinical uses, and immunomodulatory effects (C15-C26) is well-supported by appropriate citations. The characterization of BPs as suitable drug repurposing candidates (C27-C29) is reasonable given their established safety profile and accessibility. This provides appropriate scientific context for investigating BPs in COVID-19.

result: The discussion proposes multiple potential mechanisms for BP effects on COVID-19: (1) statins and amino-BPs both inhibit the mevalonate pathway but at different steps (HMG-CoA reductase vs FPPS), affecting protein prenylation and endosomal maturation; (2) amino-BPs cause IPP accumulation that stimulates Vγ9Vδ2 T cells, which play roles in antiviral defense; (3) BPs affect NK cells, regulatory T cells, and neutrophil function; (4) dysregulated neutrophil activation is implicated in severe COVID-19. The authors note that BP effects persist despite concomitant statin use, suggesting mechanisms beyond Vγ9Vδ2 T cell stimulation.
evaluation: The mechanistic discussion (C123-C139) is well-grounded in prior literature with appropriate citations, but remains speculative regarding COVID-19 specifically. The observation that BP effects are not altered by statin co-administration (C133) is interesting and argues against a simple mevalonate pathway explanation, but the alternative mechanisms proposed are not directly tested in this study. The discussion appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about which mechanisms might be operative (C139) but cannot distinguish between true immunomodulatory effects and unmeasured confounding as explanations for the observed associations.

result: The authors compare their findings to four other retrospective studies examining BPs and COVID-19 outcomes. One Turkish study (n=1,997) found no differences in hospitalization or mortality among COVID-19 patients receiving anti-osteoporosis medications. An Italian study found no difference in COVID-19 hospitalization rates between oral amino-BP users and non-users. A Spanish study found lower COVID-19 incidence with zoledronate but not oral BPs. An Israeli study found reduced COVID-19 hospitalizations among BP users (OR 0.567-0.705).
evaluation: The comparison to prior studies (C88-C90) is accurate and appropriately nuanced. The authors correctly note that their study differs in sample size (orders of magnitude larger), endpoints examined (including testing and diagnosis, not just hospitalization/mortality among diagnosed patients), and findings (consistent protective associations with oral BPs). The mixed results across studies highlight the need for prospective trials to resolve the question definitively.

result: The authors note that statins have been associated with lower mortality in hospitalized COVID-19 patients and are being tested in clinical trials. In their primary cohort, 15.2% of statin users concomitantly used BPs, and stratification by BP use within statin users showed that decreased odds of COVID-19 outcomes remained regardless of statin use.
evaluation: The statin comparison (C119-C122) is appropriate and strengthens the argument that BP effects are independent of statin use. However, the analysis doesn't fully address whether the statin-BP interaction might be more complex than simple independence. The observation that BPs show stronger associations than statins despite both affecting the mevalonate pathway is intriguing but could reflect differences in patient populations rather than drug mechanisms.

result: The authors address endpoint validity by noting that ICD-10 code U07.1 has 94% positive predictive value for COVID-19 and captured >97% of COVID-19 diagnoses across all cohorts. They note that 75-95% of US women aged 60-79 have low bone mass or osteoporosis, and women aged 60+ represent ~75% of their study population, arguing that most BP non-users in the matched cohort likely had indications for BP therapy.
evaluation: The endpoint validation (C114-C115) appropriately addresses potential misclassification of COVID-19 cases. The argument about osteoporosis prevalence (C116-C118) attempts to address the positivity assumption violation in propensity score matching, but this remains a limitation since actual bone density measurements are not available for non-users. The high prevalence of osteoporosis in the matched population makes the positivity assumption more plausible but doesn't eliminate the concern.

result: The authors note that BPs are globally available as affordable generics that are generally well-tolerated, though rare severe adverse events (osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femur fractures) are associated with long-term therapy.
evaluation: The characterization of BP availability, tolerability, and adverse events (C143-C144) is accurate and appropriately balanced. This information is relevant for considering BPs as potential prophylactic agents, though the risk-benefit calculation would depend on demonstrating actual efficacy in prospective trials.

result: The observation period (March 1 - June 30, 2020) was chosen to coincide with the first wave of COVID-19 in the US and predate vaccines or effective treatments that could modify outcomes.
evaluation: The rationale for the observation period (C30-C31) is appropriate and ensures that results are not confounded by vaccines or treatments that became available later. This temporal restriction strengthens internal validity but limits generalizability to later pandemic periods with different viral variants, vaccination rates, and treatment options.
